summary: Describes UTF-8, a way to encode the characters of ISO 10646 that keeps the US-ASCII range unchanged, so software that expects ASCII keeps working. It replaces RFC 2044 and was replaced by RFC 3629.

plainLanguage.summary: UTF-8 is a way of writing text in bytes. It can hold every character in the international character standard, and it leaves ordinary ASCII text exactly as it was, so old software keeps working with text that contains nothing else.

subtitle: The encoding that keeps plain ASCII text unchanged while adding the characters of the world's writing systems.

tldr.problem: The character set standard defines every writing system in the world, but its own encodings use four or two bytes per character, which breaks software and protocols that assume 8-bit or 7-bit bytes.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-8 encodes each character as a sequence of one to six octets, with the length and the shape of the leading octet determined by the character's number. Characters below 128 encode as a single octet with the same value as in ASCII, and octets with those values can never mean anything else.

sections.title: Why UTF-8
sections.content:
ISO/IEC 10646-1 defines a multi-octet character set called the Universal Character Set, which encompasses most of the world's writing systems. Multi-octet characters are not compatible with many current applications and protocols, which led to the development of a few UCS transformation formats, each with different characteristics.

Two multi-octet encodings are defined in the standard: UCS-4, four octets per character, and UCS-2, two octets per character, able to address only the first 64K characters of the UCS, the Basic Multilingual Plane. The same set of characters is defined by the Unicode standard, which further defines character properties and other application details, and changes in Unicode and amendments to ISO/IEC 10646 have tracked each other so that the character repertoires and code point assignments have remained in sync.

The UCS-2 and UCS-4 encodings are hard to use in applications and protocols that assume 8 or even 7 bit characters, and even newer systems able to deal with 16 bit characters cannot process UCS-4 data. That led to the transformation formats: UTF-1 has only historical interest, having been removed from ISO/IEC 10646; UTF-7 encodes the full Basic Multilingual Plane using only octets with the high-order bit clear and is therefore mail-safe; UTF-8 uses all bits of an octet but preserves the full US-ASCII range, so that US-ASCII characters are encoded in one octet having the normal US-ASCII value, and any octet with such a value can only stand for a US-ASCII character and nothing else; and UTF-16 transforms a subset of the UCS-4 repertoire into pairs of UCS-2 values from a reserved range.

UTF-8 was originally a project of the X/Open Joint Internationalization Group with the objective of specifying a file system safe UCS transformation format compatible with UNIX systems. The original authors were Gary Miller, Greger Leijonhufvud and John Entenmann, and Ken Thompson and Rob Pike later did significant work on the formal UTF-8. The definitive reference, including provisions for UTF-16 data within UTF-8, is Annex R of ISO/IEC 10646-1.
sections.plainLanguage: The international character standard needed an encoding that old software could handle. UTF-8 was designed so that plain ASCII text is byte-for-byte identical in both, which is what lets it be added to existing systems.

sections.title: How UTF-8 Encodes Characters
sections.content:
In UTF-8, characters are encoded using sequences of one to six octets. The only octet of a sequence of one has the higher-order bit set to zero, the remaining 7 bits being used to encode the character value. In a sequence of n octets with n greater than one, the initial octet has the n higher-order bits set to one followed by a bit set to zero, and the remaining bits of that octet contain bits from the value of the character. The following octets all have the higher-order bit set to one and the following bit set to zero, leaving 6 bits in each to contain bits from the character value.

The table of ranges and octet patterns is as follows, where the letter x indicates bits available for encoding bits of the UCS-4 character value: the range 0000 0000 to 0000 007F is encoded as 0xxxxxxx; 0000 0080 to 0000 07FF as 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx; 0000 0800 to 0000 FFFF as 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx; 0001 0000 to 001F FFFF as 11110xxx followed by three continuation octets; 0020 0000 to 03FF FFFF as 111110xx followed by four continuation octets; and 0400 0000 to 7FFF FFFF as 1111110x followed by continuation octets.

Encoding from UCS-4 to UTF-8 proceeds in three steps. Determine the number of octets required from the character value and the first column of the table; the rows are mutually exclusive, so there is only one valid way to encode a given character. Prepare the high-order bits of the octets as per the second column. Then fill in the bits marked x from the bits of the character value, starting from the lower-order bits of the character value and putting them first in the last octet of the sequence, then the next to last, and so on until all x bits are filled in.

Decoding from UTF-8 to UCS-4 proceeds in three steps as well: initialize the 4 octets of the character with all bits set to zero, determine which bits encode the character value from the number of octets in the sequence, and distribute the bits from the sequence to the character, first the lower-order bits from the last octet of the sequence and proceeding to the left until no x bits are left. If the UTF-8 sequence is no more than three octets long, decoding can proceed directly to UCS-2.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte of a character says how many bytes the character uses, and the value of the character is spread across the free bits of the bytes that follow. That is why the leading byte patterns are what they are.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The UCS-2 sequence for the string A, followed by the not identical to sign, followed by the Greek capital letter alpha, followed by a full stop, with code points 0041, 2262, 0391 and 002E, is encoded in UTF-8 as 41 E2 89 A2 CE 91 2E.

The UCS-2 sequence representing the Hangul characters for the Korean word hangugo, with code points D55C, AD6D and C5B4, is encoded as ED 95 9C EA B5 AD EC 96 B4.

The UCS-2 sequence representing the Han characters for the Japanese word nihongo, with code points 65E5, 672C and 8A9E, is encoded as E6 97 A5 E6 9C AC E8 AA 9E.
sections.plainLanguage: Each example shows the same thing at three scales: one ASCII letter takes one byte, a Greek letter takes two, a Hangul syllable takes three and a Japanese character takes three as well.

sections.title: Versions of the Standards
sections.content:
ISO/IEC 10646 is updated from time to time by published amendments, and different versions of the Unicode standard exist. Each new version obsoletes and replaces the previous one, but implementations, and more significantly data, are not updated instantly. In general the changes amount to adding new characters, which does not pose particular problems for old data.

Amendment 5 to ISO/IEC 10646 is the exception: it moved and expanded the Korean Hangul block, thereby making any previous data containing Hangul characters invalid under the new version, and Unicode 2.0 has the same difference from Unicode 1.1. The official justification for allowing such an incompatible change was that no implementations and no data containing Hangul existed, a statement that is likely to be true but remains unprovable. The incident has been dubbed the Korean mess, and the relevant committees have pledged never to make such an incompatible change again.
sections.plainLanguage: Character sets grow by adding characters, which is safe. One amendment moved the Hangul block and broke existing data, an episode known as the Korean mess.

sections.title: The MIME Charset Label
sections.content:
The memo is the basis for registering a MIME character set parameter, and the proposed charset parameter value is UTF-8. The string labels media types containing text consisting of characters from the repertoire of ISO/IEC 10646 including all amendments at least up to amendment 5, the Korean block, encoded with the scheme described above. UTF-8 is suitable for use in MIME content types under the text top-level type.

The label UTF-8 does not contain a version identification, referring generically to ISO/IEC 10646, and this is intentional. A MIME charset label is designed to give just the information needed to interpret a sequence of bytes received on the wire into a sequence of characters, nothing more. As long as a character set standard does not change incompatibly, version numbers serve no purpose, because one gains nothing by learning from the tag that newly assigned characters may be received that one does not know about.

There is, however, a disadvantage to version-dependent labels: when an older application receives data accompanied by a newer unknown label, it may fail to recognise the label and be completely unable to deal with the data, whereas a generic known label would have triggered mostly correct processing. The Korean mess is in principle a contradiction of the version-independent label, but the compatibility problem can only appear with data containing Hangul syllables encoded according to Unicode 1.1, and there is arguably no such data to worry about.

It is also proposed to register the charset parameter value UNICODE-1-1-UTF-8, for the exclusive purpose of labelling text data containing Hangul syllables encoded to UTF-8 without taking into account amendment 5 of ISO/IEC 10646. Any other UTF-8 data should not use this label, in particular data not containing any Hangul syllables, and the RFC strongly recommends against creating any new Hangul-containing data without taking amendment 5 into account.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIME label is simply UTF-8, with no version number, so that old software still recognises it. A separate label exists only for the old Hangul code points that the Korean mess broke.

sections.title: Illegal Sequences and Security
sections.content:
Implementors of UTF-8 need to consider the security aspects of how they handle illegal UTF-8 sequences. It is conceivable that in some circumstances an attacker would be able to exploit an incautious UTF-8 parser by sending it an octet sequence that is not permitted by the UTF-8 syntax.

A particularly subtle form of this attack could be carried out against a parser that performs security-critical validity checks against the UTF-8 encoded form of its input, but interprets certain illegal octet sequences as characters. For example, a parser might prohibit the NUL character when encoded as the single octet sequence 00, but allow the illegal two-octet sequence C0 80 and interpret it as a NUL character. Another example might be a parser that prohibits the octet sequence 2F 2E 2E 2F, the path sequence /../, yet permits the illegal octet sequence 2F C0 AE 2E 2F.
sections.plainLanguage: A parser that rejects a dangerous byte sequence in its normal form but accepts a malformed variant of it can be bypassed. The RFC's advice is to reject illegal UTF-8 sequences rather than decode them leniently.

viz.caption: THE PROPERTIES THAT MADE UTF-8 USEFUL

items.title: ASCII stays ASCII
items.text: Characters below 128 are one octet with the same value, so plain ASCII text is also valid UTF-8.

items.title: No accidental ASCII
items.text: Octets with ASCII values never appear inside a multi-octet character.

items.title: Self-synchronizing
items.text: Character boundaries can be found from anywhere in a byte stream.

items.title: Easy round trip
items.text: Converting between UTF-8 and UCS-2 or UCS-4 is straightforward in both directions.
